title: The Impact of Schoolyard Greening on Children's Physical Activity and Socioemotional Health: A Systematic Review of Experimental Studies
review_question: To examine the impact of schoolyard greening on measures of physical activity and socioemotional health in children, specifically focusing on experimental studies.
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: P (Population): Children under 18. I (Intervention): Greening the schoolyard or daycare yard and exposure of children pre/post-greening. C (Comparison): All types of control (other schools without green schoolyards) or self-controls (changes over time within same subjects). O (Outcomes): Physical activity and/or socioemotional health. S (Study design): Only experimental and/or quasi-experimental studies. Excluded: Non-experimental studies, studies without schoolyard greening intervention or children's exposure, reviews, protocols, studies without PA or SEH outcomes, non-English language.

findings.quote: Schoolyard greening was associated with a beneficial change in children's PA in many, although not all, PA outcome measures.

findings.consequent: Time spent in light physical activity (PA)
findings.quote: Raney at al. and Hamer at al. reported no significant change in overall time spent in light PA post-greening, though Hamer at al. found an increase of time spent in light PA for students younger than nine.

findings.consequent: Time spent in moderate to vigorous physical activity (MVPA)
findings.quote: Two studies found that schoolyard greening significantly stimulates physical activity in girls by increasing the amount of time they spent in MVPA during recess, particularly shortly after greening.
Hamer et al. examined an intervention to install AstroTurf only... found a decrease in time spent sedentary for children younger than nine.
Raney at al. also looked at schoolyard utilization and found positive associations between schoolyard greening and increase in utilization of greened areas in the schoolyard.
Three studies found a positive or mixed association between schoolyard greening and some children's prosocial behaviors.
Raney et al. observed a significant decrease in physical and verbal conflicts after greening.

findings.consequent: Appreciation of the greenyard (naturalness, likability, attractiveness, perceived restorative quality)
findings.quote: children showed greater appreciation of the greened schoolyard, particularly younger children and girls.
Two studies found a positive association between schoolyard greening and attention restoration.
no impact was observed for another measure, executive functioning.

findings.consequent: Mental well-being (emotional well-being, intrapsychic balance, depression score)
findings.quote: Three studies found a positive association between schoolyard greening and mental well-being... One study found no greening impact on children's emotional well-being.

synthesis_conclusions: Schoolyard greening generally has a positive impact on children's physical activity and socioemotional health outcomes.
Greening schoolyards is a viable intervention to reduce health equity gaps and improve children's health regardless of background or socioeconomic status.
Greening promotes equal play opportunities for male and female students, potentially addressing physical activity equity gaps.
Early exposure to green space through greened schoolyards is a promising venue for reducing health inequities.
evidence_gaps: Need for more robust experimental evidence regarding the impact of greening on physical activity and socioemotional health outcomes.
Future studies should use more rigorous approaches in methodology, data collection, and analysis to limit sources of error.
Need for studies including multiple days of data collection and combining observational tools (SOPLAY, SOCARP) with GPS and accelerometer data.
Need for quasi-experimental studies with comparison groups and prospective observation of student cohorts.
Need for longitudinal studies investigating health benefits of early and equitable access to green schoolyards.
Need for studies looking at sex-specific and age-group-specific PA levels in green schoolyards.
risk_of_bias_assessment: Not formally assessed for the review itself; individual study limitations (e.g., quasi-experimental design, selection bias, limited data collection) were discussed.
heterogeneity_sources: Methodological approaches (study design, data collection techniques, sample sizes)
Specific outcome measures and their definitions
Quantity and quality of greening intervention

moderators.effect: Younger children (under 9) showed increased light PA and decreased sedentary time. Younger children and girls showed greater appreciation of greenyards and positive social functioning. Older children showed negative effects on prosocial behavior.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Increased light PA for kids under 9; decreased sedentary time for kids under 9; greater greenyard appreciation for younger children; positive social functioning for younger children; negative prosocial behavior for older children.

moderators.effect: Girls showed increased MVPA and greater appreciation of greenyards, while boys showed no impact on PA in some studies.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Increased MVPA for girls; greater greenyard appreciation for girls; no PA impact for boys in some studies.

moderators.effect: Beneficial effects on attention restoration were observed longer after greening (second time point). Positive PA changes were particularly noted shortly after greening.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Attention restoration effects observed at second follow-up; PA increases particularly shortly after greening.

limitations: The review only included studies published in the English language.
The heterogeneity in findings suggests the need for more robust experimental evidence.
Current studies often lack rigorous methodological approaches, data collection, and analysis to limit sources of error.

paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: Access to green schoolyards (schoolyards designed with greenery and natural elements to create a park-like environment, as opposed to asphalt-based playgrounds) are associated with many benefits for students, including improvements in physical and mental health. While many studies examining these associations are cross-sectional, some feature experimental designs that offer the possibility of causal inference. In this review, we looked at experimental studies that examine the impact of schoolyard greening on measures of physical activity and socioemotional health in children. Four electronic databases (Ovid Medline, PsycINFO, Scopus and Greenfile) were searched, and from 1843 articles retrieved, 6 articles met the inclusion criteria. Examination of the eligible studies revealed a general consensus on the positive impact of schoolyard greening on both physical activity and socioemotional health outcomes for students, suggesting that schoolyard greening is a viable intervention in reducing the health equity gaps and improving children’s health regardless of their racial or ethnic backgrounds or residential neighborhood socioeconomic status. Further experimental research on this topic should elucidate how educators, administrators, policy makers, and other stakeholders can harness the benefits of schoolyard greening to improve the health and well-being of children in their communities.
